lead: This unit turns calculus loose on fields: functions that fill space with a number or an arrow at every point. You learn the three jobs of the del operator — gradient, divergence, curl — and then the three big theorems that trade an integral over a boundary for an integral over the region inside. By the end you can test a field for solenoidality, find a scalar potential, compute work, flux and volume integrals, and use Green's, Stokes' and Gauss's theorems to replace a hard integral with an easy one.
about: Chapters 6.1 and 6.2 build the toolkit: the gradient gives the direction of steepest rise and the normal to a surface, while divergence and curl measure source strength and rotation. Chapter 6.3 uses those two tests to sort fields into solenoidal and irrotational, and to recover a scalar potential by integration. Chapters 6.4 and 6.5 integrate along curves, over surfaces and through solids, which is where work and flux appear. Chapters 6.6, 6.7 and 6.8 give the three conversion theorems — Green in the plane, Stokes on a surface, Gauss in a volume — each turning a boundary integral into an interior one. Chapter 6.9, taught in only a few universities, describes how a space curve bends and twists.

chapters.idea: The gradient is a vector that points where a scalar field rises fastest, and its size is that fastest rate; the directional derivative is just the gradient projected on a chosen unit direction.
chapters.depth: Scalar field φ(x, y, z). Gradient ∇φ = φ_x i + φ_y j + φ_z k as a vector. Level surfaces φ = constant and the fact that ∇φ is normal to them. Directional derivative D_û φ = ∇φ·û, with û a unit vector; maximum rate |∇φ| along ∇φ, minimum rate −|∇φ|. Unit normal to a surface f(x, y, z) = constant as ∇f/|∇f|. Angle between two surfaces as the angle between their normals, using cos θ = (n₁·n₂)/(|n₁||n₂|). Some syllabi give the direction as a vector a rather than a unit vector, and some call the directional derivative the derivative along a direction — show both forms. Work only in three variables, with a two-variable case as a remark.

figure.title: From a scalar field to a directional derivative
figure.aria: A downward flow from a scalar field through the gradient and a unit direction to the directional derivative, with the maximum rate and the surface normal branching off the gradient.

chapters.example: A scalar field is φ = x²y + 2yz. Find the directional derivative of φ at P(1, 2, −1) in the direction of a = i + 2j + 2k, and the maximum rate of increase at P. The partial derivatives are φ_x = 2xy, φ_y = x² + 2z, φ_z = 2y, so ∇φ = (4, −1, 4) at P. |a| = √(1 + 4 + 4) = 3, so û = (1/3, 2/3, 2/3). Then D_û φ = (4×1 − 1×2 + 4×2)/3 = 10/3 ≈ 3.33 per unit length. The maximum rate is |∇φ| = √(16 + 1 + 16) = √33 ≈ 5.74 per unit length, in the direction (4, −1, 4).
chapters.trap: Forgetting to divide the direction vector by its length. Dividing component by component instead of by |a| gives a wrong answer here (the length is 3, not 1), and the maximum rate is often missed even when the directional derivative is right.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4: partial derivatives, and tangent planes and normal lines to surfaces.
chapters.leave: Tangent planes, normal lines and maxima/minima of functions of several variables stay in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The single operator ∇ acts in three ways: on a scalar it gives a vector (gradient), dotted with a vector it gives a scalar (divergence), crossed with a vector it gives a vector (curl).
chapters.depth: Definition of ∇ = i ∂/∂x + j ∂/∂y + k ∂/∂z. div F = ∇·F = ∂F₁/∂x + ∂F₂/∂y + ∂F₃/∂z, a scalar. curl F = ∇×F written as a determinant, a vector. Physical reading: divergence as outward flux per unit volume (positive at a source, negative at a sink), curl as circulation per unit area (twice the local angular velocity of a tiny paddle wheel). Product rules for div and curl of φF. Identities to prove by expansion: div(curl F) = 0, curl(∇φ) = 0, div(∇φ) = ∇²φ. Mention curl(curl F) = ∇(∇·F) − ∇²F in one line. Exam wording is usually 'prove that' for the two zero identities.

figure.aria: One del operator branching into gradient, divergence and curl, showing the input and output type of each.

chapters.example: For F = (xy, yz, zx), find div F and curl F at the point (1, 2, 3), and check that div(curl F) = 0. div F = ∂(xy)/∂x + ∂(yz)/∂y + ∂(zx)/∂z = y + z + x, which is 6 at (1, 2, 3). curl F = (∂F₃/∂y − ∂F₂/∂z, ∂F₁/∂z − ∂F₃/∂x, ∂F₂/∂x − ∂F₁/∂y) = (0 − y, 0 − z, 0 − x) = (−2, −3, −1) at the point. Then div(curl F) = ∂(−y)/∂x + ∂(−z)/∂y + ∂(−x)/∂z = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, as the identity promises.
chapters.trap: The middle component of the curl carries a minus sign: it is ∂F₁/∂z − ∂F₃/∂x. Students also report divergence as a vector or curl as a scalar; the types are fixed and the identity check catches some of these slips.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for the del operator and partial derivatives from Unit 4.
chapters.leave: The Laplacian as the main object of Laplace's and Poisson's equations belongs to a later PDE course.

chapters.idea: A field with zero divergence is solenoidal, a field with zero curl is irrotational, and an irrotational field is the gradient of a scalar potential that you find by integrating and matching.
chapters.depth: Definitions over a region: F is solenoidal when div F = 0; F is irrotational when curl F = 0. For irrotational F there is a scalar potential φ with F = ∇φ. Method: integrate F₁ with respect to x, add an unknown function g(y, z), differentiate the result with respect to y and z, compare with F₂ and F₃, and fix g. φ is unique only up to an additive constant, so report φ + C. Show the reverse check: if F = ∇φ then curl F = 0. Add one line that the region must have no holes for the converse to hold everywhere — only a few syllabi press this point. State clearly that an irrotational field is conservative and its line integrals are path independent, which 6.4 uses.

figure.title: Testing a field and building its potential
figure.aria: A test flow that checks divergence and curl of a field and then integrates the field to produce a scalar potential plus a constant.

chapters.example: Show that F = (2xy + z², x² + 2yz, y² + 2zx) is irrotational and find its scalar potential. curl F = (2y − 2y, 2z − 2z, 2x − 2x) = 0, so the field is irrotational. Put ∂φ/∂x = 2xy + z², so φ = x²y + xz² + g(y, z). Then ∂φ/∂y = x² + g_y = x² + 2yz gives g_y = 2yz, so g = y²z + h(z). Next ∂φ/∂z = 2xz + y² + h′(z) = y² + 2zx, so h′(z) = 0. Hence φ = x²y + y²z + z²x + C, and φ = 3 + C at (1, 1, 1).
chapters.trap: Declaring a field irrotational or solenoidal from its value at one point; the condition must hold at every point of the region. Dropping the + C, or forgetting that the unknown after the first integration may depend on both remaining variables, costs marks.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for divergence and curl; partial integration from Unit 2.
chapters.leave: The proof that path independence follows from curl F = 0 is done in 6.4.

chapters.idea: A line integral adds up the component of a field along a curve, and for a force field that sum is the work done.
chapters.depth: Definition ∫_C F·dr = ∫_C (F₁ dx + F₂ dy + F₃ dz). Parameterise the curve: r(t) = (x(t), y(t), z(t)), dr = r′(t) dt, and integrate in t from the start value to the end value. Work done by F along C as ∫_C F·dr with F a force. Closed curve gives circulation ∮_C F·dr. Path independence: in the plane the test is ∂N/∂x = ∂M/∂y for F = (M, N); in space it is curl F = 0, and then F = ∇φ and ∫_C F·dr = φ(end) − φ(start). Show one example where two different paths give two different answers. Keep the fundamental-theorem shortcut brief; 6.3 supplies the potential.

figure.aria: Two different routes from point A to point B plus a straight route, showing that the work done depends on which path is taken.

chapters.example: Evaluate the work ∫_C F·dr for F = (x + y, y − x) from (0, 0) to (1, 1) along the parabola y = x². Take x = t, y = t² with t from 0 to 1, so dr = (1, 2t) dt and F = (t + t², t² − t). Then F·dr = (t + t²) + (t² − t)(2t) = t − t² + 2t³, and the integral from 0 to 1 is 1/2 − 1/3 + 1/2 = 2/3. Along the straight line y = x the same field gives F·dr = 2t dt and the integral 1. The answers differ, so the field is not conservative — indeed ∂N/∂x = −1 while ∂M/∂y = 1.
chapters.trap: Writing dx dy or dA where dr belongs, and reversing the direction of travel (which flips the sign). Students also compare two paths without first checking that the field is non-conservative, so the difference surprises them.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for definite integrals and arc length; 6.1 for the gradient of a potential.
chapters.leave: Line integrals around closed curves are converted to double integrals in 6.6.

chapters.idea: A surface integral adds a field over a curved sheet, a volume integral adds it through a solid, and both are ordinary multiple integrals once the geometry is written down.
chapters.depth: Surface integral of a scalar, ∬_S φ dS, and of a vector field, ∬_S F·n dS, the flux. The area element for a graph z = f(x, y) is dS = √(1 + f_x² + f_y²) dA; for a plane g(x, y, z) = c use the unit normal n = ∇g/|∇g|. Orientation: choose n, and for a closed surface take it outward. Volume integral ∭_V f dV as a triple integral, with the limits from the shape. Some syllabi call the vector surface integral a flux integral. Keep each evaluation to a shape whose projection is a triangle, a rectangle or a disk.

figure.aria: Nested regions: a curve lies inside a surface, which lies inside a solid, each carrying its own kind of integral.

chapters.example: Find the flux ∬_S F·n dS for F = (x, y, z) across the part S of the plane x + y + z = 1 lying in the first octant, with n pointing away from the origin. Here g = x + y + z, ∇g = (1, 1, 1) and |∇g| = √3, so n = (1, 1, 1)/√3. On the plane F·n = (x + y + z)/√3 = 1/√3. Since z = 1 − x − y, dS = √(1 + 1 + 1) dA = √3 dA. So the flux is ∬ (1/√3)(√3) dA = ∬ dA = area of the triangle with intercepts 1, 1, 1, which is 1/2. As a check, ∭_V div F dV over the tetrahedron is 3 × (1/6) = 1/2, the same number — this is Gauss's theorem from 6.8.
chapters.trap: Using dA in place of dS and forgetting the factor √(1 + f_x² + f_y²), or using a non-unit normal so that F·n is scaled wrongly. A sign error in the direction of n flips the whole answer.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for double and triple integrals and their limits; 6.1 for the unit normal to a surface.
chapters.leave: Change of variables and Jacobians for these integrals are covered in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Green's theorem replaces a line integral round a closed plane curve by a double integral over the region it encloses.
chapters.depth: Statement: if C is the anticlockwise boundary of a plane region R and M, N have continuous first partials on R, then ∮_C (M dx + N dy) = ∬_R (∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y) dA. Explain positive orientation with a sketch in words. Use it both ways: a hard line integral becomes an easy area integral, and sometimes the reverse. Derive the area formula A = ½∮_C (x dy − y dx) in one line. Verify on a rectangle or a triangle by computing both sides. Say that C may be piecewise smooth and that R may have a hole if both boundaries are oriented correctly.

figure.title: Green's theorem in one line
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain from a plane region to its boundary curve, then to the line integral, which equals the double integral of Nx minus My.

chapters.example: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ∮_C (x² − y²) dx + 2xy dy, where C is the boundary of the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 taken anticlockwise. Here M = x² − y² and N = 2xy, so ∂N/∂x = 2y and ∂M/∂y = −2y, giving ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y = 4y. Then ∬_R 4y dA = ∫₀² dx ∫₀¹ 4y dy = 2 × 2 = 4. The line integral has the same value 4, but needs four separate edges.
chapters.trap: Writing ∂M/∂y − ∂N/∂x and losing a sign, and using a clockwise curve without changing the sign of the answer. A curve that is not closed cannot be handled by Green's theorem at all.
chapters.prereq: 6.4 for line integrals; Unit 5 for double integrals over a rectangle or triangle.
chapters.leave: The three-dimensional version — a curve on a surface — is 6.7.

chapters.idea: Stokes' theorem says the circulation of a field round the boundary of a surface equals the flux of its curl through the surface.
chapters.depth: Statement: for an open surface S with unit normal n and boundary C, oriented by the right-hand rule, ∮_C F·dr = ∬_S (∇×F)·n dS. Explain the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand along C and the thumb gives n. Emphasise that S may be curved and that any surface with the same boundary gives the same answer. Show that a flat S in the plane z = 0 reduces the statement to Green's theorem. Evaluate one circulation both ways, and one surface integral by choosing a convenient flat surface.

figure.title: Stokes' theorem and its orientation rule
figure.aria: A surface with its normal and boundary curve feeds a circulation integral that equals the flux of the curl, with an orientation link back to the start.

chapters.example: Verify Stokes' theorem for F = (−y, x, 0) on the disk S of radius 2 in the plane z = 0, with n = k and C the circle x² + y² = 4 taken anticlockwise. curl F = (0, 0, 2), so ∬_S (∇×F)·n dS = 2 × (area 4π) = 8π. On the boundary r(t) = (2cos t, 2sin t, 0) with t from 0 to 2π, dr = (−2sin t, 2cos t, 0) dt and F = (−2sin t, 2cos t, 0), so F·dr = 4sin²t + 4cos²t = 4. Then ∮ F·dr = ∫₀^{2π} 4 dt = 8π. Both sides agree.
chapters.trap: Mismatching the orientation of C and n, which flips one side only, and plugging the flat normal k into a curved surface. The curl must be computed before the dot product with n, not after.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for curl, 6.4 for line integrals, 6.5 for surface integrals, 6.6 for the flat case.

chapters.idea: Gauss's divergence theorem says the outward flux of a field through a closed surface equals the integral of its divergence through the enclosed volume.
chapters.depth: Statement: for a closed surface S bounding a solid V, with n the outward unit normal, ∬_S F·n dS = ∭_V (∇·F) dV. Conditions: F smooth, S closed and piecewise smooth. Use it in both directions: a sum of six face integrals becomes one volume integral, and a volume integral of a divergence becomes a flux. Verify on a cube. Give the physical reading — divergence is the source density, so the total flux out equals the total source inside — and name two places it appears: Gauss's law for electric field, and the continuity equation for a conserved quantity such as water flow in a tank. Keep applications to one line each.

figure.aria: A ladder of conversion theorems from the fundamental theorem on an interval up through Green and Stokes to Gauss in a volume.

chapters.example: Verify the divergence theorem for F = (x², y², z²) over the unit cube V = [0, 1]³ with S its boundary. div F = 2x + 2y + 2z, so ∭_V div F dV = 2∫₀¹x dx + 2∫₀¹y dy + 2∫₀¹z dz = 2(1/2) + 2(1/2) + 2(1/2) = 3, using that each single integral is 1/2 and the other two integrate to 1. For the flux, the face x = 1 has n = i and F·n = 1, giving flux 1; the face x = 0 has F·n = −x² = 0. The same happens for the y and z pairs, so the total flux is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Both sides agree.
chapters.trap: Using the inward normal, or applying the theorem to an open surface that does not enclose a volume. On a cube, students also forget the two faces where the field is zero and double-count the others.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for divergence; 6.5 for surface and volume integrals.
chapters.leave: Applications to electrostatics and fluid flow beyond one line.

chapters.idea: A space curve has a tangent and a normal at each point, and two numbers — curvature and torsion — record how fast it turns and how fast it twists out of its plane.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Parameterised curve r(t); arc length s = ∫|r′(t)| dt; unit tangent T = r′/|r′|; principal normal N = T′/|T′|; binormal B = T×N. Curvature κ = |dT/ds| = |r′×r″|/|r′|³, with units of 1/length; torsion τ = (r′×r″·r‴)/|r′×r″|². State the Frenet–Serret formulas T′ = κN, N′ = −κT + τB, B′ = −τN without deriving them. Straight line: κ = 0. Circle of radius a: κ = 1/a, τ = 0. Keep the chapter short: one worked helix, one formula list.

figure.aria: Two flat horizontal lines at 0.4 and 0.2 showing that the helix keeps the same curvature and the same torsion at every parameter value.

chapters.example: For the helix r(t) = (2cos t, 2sin t, t), find the curvature and torsion. r′ = (−2sin t, 2cos t, 1) so |r′| = √5. r″ = (−2cos t, −2sin t, 0) and r‴ = (2sin t, −2cos t, 0). Then r′×r″ = (2sin t, −2cos t, 4), whose length is √20 = 2√5. So κ = 2√5/(√5)³ = 2√5/(5√5) = 2/5 = 0.4. Also (r′×r″)·r‴ = 4sin²t + 4cos²t + 0 = 4, and |r′×r″|² = 20, so τ = 4/20 = 1/5 = 0.2. Both numbers are the same at every t, which is why the plot is two flat lines.
chapters.trap: Using |r′|² in the denominator of the curvature instead of |r′|³, and forgetting to divide r′ by |r′| before differentiating to get T. Torsion comes out with the wrong sign if the cross product order is swapped.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for arc length; Unit 4 for derivatives of vector-valued functions.
chapters.leave: Frenet–Serret derivations and the differential geometry of surfaces belong to a later course.
